steps.label: Information
steps.body:
```
opposable thumbs → primate
primate indigenous to Madagascar → lemur
lemur → lower primate
living diurnal lower primate → lemur (certain species)
higher primate → thought to have evolved from one diurnal lower-primate species
```

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On a Must Be True question, we look for a concept that shows up more than once and try to link through it. Here the bridge is "lemur." The only primates native to Madagascar are lemurs, and lemurs are lower primates. Put those together: every primate native to Madagascar is a lower primate.

Now ask what that rules out. Lower primates and higher primates are two separate groups, so a lower primate is not a higher primate. That means no primate native to Madagascar is a higher primate. Not a diurnal one, not a nocturnal one, not any kind.

The last sentence is the tempting one, because it looks like it chains with the lemur sentence. Higher primates are thought to have evolved from one diurnal lower-primate species, and certain lemurs are the only living diurnal lower primates. Does that make the ancestor a lemur? No. The lemur claim covers only living lower primates, and the ancestor could be a species that no longer exists. On top of that, "are thought to have evolved" only reports what people believe. Nothing about ancestry is proven here.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Predict the Madagascar chain: no primate native to Madagascar is a higher primate.

Expect the answer to dress that up. If an answer adds a detail that only narrows the group of higher primates (say, diurnal ones), it is still proven: if no higher primate is native to Madagascar, no smaller slice of higher primates is either. Be suspicious of any answer that treats the ancestral species and the lemurs as the same thing.

notes.body: This treats the ancestral species as a lemur. The passage says higher primates are thought to have evolved from one diurnal lower-primate species, and that certain lemurs are the only living diurnal lower primates. The ancestor could be an extinct species that was never a lemur. And "thought to have evolved" is a belief, not an established fact, so no claim about chimpanzee ancestry has to be true.

This is the chain from the Goal. Lemurs are the only primates indigenous to Madagascar, and lemurs are lower primates, so every primate native to Madagascar is a lower primate and none is a higher primate. B narrows that to "diurnal higher primates," which changes nothing. If no higher primate is native to Madagascar, no diurnal higher primate is either.

The move to carry forward: when an answer adds a qualifier to a "none" statement you've proven, check whether the qualifier only shrinks the group. A smaller slice of an excluded group is still excluded.

The passage describes the ancestor, not the descendants. Even if every higher primate came from a diurnal species, nothing stops a descendant species from being nocturnal today. The passage never says when higher primates are active now, so "no higher primate is nocturnal" doesn't have to be true.

The passage states that only primates have opposable thumbs. That means anything with opposable thumbs is a primate; it does not mean every primate has them. So the passage leaves open whether some lemurs lack opposable thumbs, but it gives no reason to think any do. With no support either way, this answer does not have to be true.

The passage says some species of lemurs are the only living lower primates that are diurnal. This means some lemur species are diurnal, but it does not say all lemurs are diurnal. The word "some" leaves open the possibility that other lemur species are nocturnal. This answer claims there are no nocturnal lemurs, which goes beyond what the passage states.

old_steps.label: Information
old_steps.body:
```
conditionals (only / the only / all)
have opposable thumbs → primate
primate indigenous → lemurs
to Madagascar
lower primates and → certain lemurs
diurnal and living
higher primate → evolved from one single
diurnal lower primate
```

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: We're trying to figure out whether we can combine any of these claims. We got multiple conditionals, but it doesn't seem like any of them chain together. What are the Overlapping Concepts? Lots. Primates, lower primates, lemurs, and diurnal all show up multiple times. Given that we were told that all higher primates evolved from a single diurnal species of lower primates, and given that some species of lemur are the only living lower primates that are diurnal, we have some support for the inference that all higher primates evolved from a lemur species, but this is Must Be True, not Most Supported. We don't know that for sure.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Look for a provable answer. It's hard to predict what it will be since this assortment of facts didn't lend itself to any obvious combining / synthesizing.

old_notes.body: The passage states that all higher primates evolved from a single diurnal lower primate species, but it never identifies that species as a lemur. The passage says some lemurs are diurnal lower primates, and higher primates evolved from a diurnal lower primate — but these could be different species of diurnal lower primates. The passage does not establish that the ancestral species was a lemur, let alone a chimpanzee's specific ancestor. Furthermore, "evolved from" describes a distant ancestral relationship, not a direct lineage claim linking chimpanzees specifically to lemurs. This inference requires assumptions beyond what the passage states.

The passage states that lemurs are the only primates indigenous to Madagascar (F3) and that lemurs are lower primates (F2). From these two facts, it follows necessarily that all primates indigenous to Madagascar are lower primates — and therefore no primates indigenous to Madagascar are higher primates. Since no higher primates are indigenous to Madagascar, no diurnal higher primates are indigenous to Madagascar either. This answer captures exactly this inference: "no primates indigenous to Madagascar are diurnal higher primates." The reasoning is airtight — if the entire set (higher primates) is excluded from Madagascar, then any subset of that set (diurnal higher primates) is also excluded. No additional assumptions are needed.

The passage says all higher primates are thought to have evolved from a single diurnal species of lower primates. This tells us the ancestral species was diurnal, but it does not tell us that all current higher primates are diurnal. Evolution from a diurnal ancestor does not guarantee that all descendants remain diurnal. Many higher primate species could have evolved nocturnal habits over millions of years. The passage provides no information about the current activity patterns of higher primates as a group — only about their evolutionary origin.

The passage states that only primates have opposable thumbs. That means anything with opposable thumbs is a primate; it does not mean every primate has them. So the passage leaves open whether some lemurs lack opposable thumbs, but it gives no reason to think any do. With no support either way, this answer does not have to be true.

The passage says some species of lemurs are the only living lower primates that are diurnal. This means some lemur species are diurnal, but it does not say all lemurs are diurnal. The word "some" leaves open the possibility that other lemur species are nocturnal. This answer claims there are no nocturnal lemurs, which goes beyond what the passage states.

steps.label: Statements
steps.body: Rational Choice Theory: The reason various political parties are popular is that individual voters make a deliberate decision to support the party they think has policies that will yield them the greatest economic advantage. Many Sociologists: This theory is wrong. A complex phenomenon such as the rise of a political organization cannot be caused by a simple phenomenon.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Match up the parts of the sociologists' response. The theory says that X (popular support for political parties) is explained by Y (individual voters deliberately backing the party whose policies they think will give them the greatest economic advantage). The sociologists object that a complex phenomenon cannot be caused by a simple phenomenon.

That objection only lands if Y is a simple phenomenon. If voters' economic decisions were themselves complex, the sociologists' rule would not touch the theory. So the sociologists apparently assume that Y is simple.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Look for an answer saying the sociologists treat voters' economically driven decisions as a simple phenomenon, or at least as something that isn't automatically complex.

The stem asks what the sociologists believe, so we can only credit them with what their objection commits them to. A modestly worded answer ("need not," "can be") is easier to prove than a sweeping one.

notes.body:
This is the belief the objection runs on. The sociologists reject the theory because a complex phenomenon can't be caused by a simple one. That only counts against rational-choice theory if the cause the theory names, voters' economically motivated decisions, is simple. So the sociologists must think those decisions are not necessarily complex. "Need not constitute a complex phenomenon" says exactly that, and says it modestly.

The move: when a group rejects a theory by citing a general rule, ask which category the rule must put the theory's key idea in. That classification is something the group has to believe.

The sociologists' rule only rules one thing out: a simple cause can't produce a complex result. It says nothing about how many causes a complex phenomenon has, or that each of them must be complex. A single complex cause would fit their rule just as well. "Many complex causes" adds a claim about number that we can't trace to anything the sociologists said.

The sociologists never say what does cause popular support for parties. They only say the theory's cause is too simple. Religion and culture never appear in the passage, so we have no basis for crediting the sociologists with this view.

This is the reverse of what they believe. Their rule is about complex phenomena, so the objection only applies if popular support for parties is complex. If they thought it was never complex, their own rule wouldn't touch the theory and the objection would collapse.

The sociologists don't deny that voters care about economic advantage. They deny that those decisions are enough, by themselves, to explain something as complex as the rise of a political organization. Someone can agree that voters chase economic advantage and still think it's too simple a cause.

old_steps.label: Statements
old_steps.body: Rational Choice Theory: The reason various political parties are popular is that individual voters make a deliberate decision to support the party they think has policies that will yield them the greatest economic advantage. Many Sociologists: This theory is wrong. A complex phenomenon such as the rise of a political party cannot be caused by a simple phenomenon.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: If we're matching up the parts of the sociologists' response, they seem to be saying that "individual voters making a deliberate decision about which party's policies would most help them economically" is a simple phenomenon. They're objecting to a theory that says "the reason for X is Y", and their objection is that "a complex thing like X can't be explained by a simple phenomenon". So they apparently assume that Y is a simple phenomenon.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Look for an answer that connects "simple phenomenon" to the idea of "individual voters deciding on which party's policies would benefits them most economically".

old_notes.body: The sociologists' argument: complex phenomena cannot be caused by simple phenomena. They apply this to reject rational-choice theory, which explains political party support (a complex phenomenon) through individual voters' economically motivated decisions. For this objection to be internally coherent, the sociologists must be classifying economically motivated voter decisions as a simple — not complex — phenomenon. If those decisions were complex, the sociologists' own principle would not apply to the situation, and the objection would fail. This answer captures exactly what the sociologists must believe: economically motivated decisions by voters need not constitute a complex phenomenon. The "need not" qualifier is appropriately modest — the sociologists believe these decisions do not automatically rise to the level of complexity, which is all that is required for their objection to function.

The sociologists' principle is that complex phenomena cannot be caused by simple phenomena. This does not mean they believe complex phenomena generally have "many complex causes." Their principle distinguishes only between simple and complex causes — it does not make a claim about the quantity of causes. A complex phenomenon might have a single complex cause, according to their logic. This answer adds a claim about multiplicity ("many complex causes") that goes beyond what the sociologists' stated principle requires. The passage gives us their principle about simple vs. complex, not a theory about how many causes complex phenomena typically have.

The passage says nothing about religious and cultural causes of political phenomena. The sociologists' objection is structural — they argue that a simple phenomenon cannot cause a complex one. They do not specify what the correct (complex) cause would be. They might believe the causes are cultural, religious, economic, social, or something else entirely — the passage provides no information about their preferred alternative explanation. This answer introduces a specific alternative causal theory that is nowhere mentioned or implied in the passage.

The sociologists' argument depends on popular support for political parties BEING a complex phenomenon. They argue: complex phenomena cannot be caused by simple phenomena; therefore, individual economic decisions (simple) cannot explain political party support (complex). If popular support were never a complex phenomenon, the sociologists' own principle would have no application to this case, and their objection would be meaningless. This answer claims the sociologists believe popular support is never complex — the exact opposite of what their argument requires. Their argument only works BECAUSE they consider it complex.

The passage describes rational-choice theory as explaining support through decisions motivated by "greatest economic advantage." The sociologists oppose the theory's causal structure, not its claim about voter motivation. Nothing in the passage suggests the sociologists believe voters are not influenced by economic considerations. They simply believe that economically motivated individual decisions — even if they exist — are too simple a cause for a complex phenomenon like the rise of political organizations. The sociologists' complaint is about simplicity vs. complexity of causal mechanisms, not about whether economic beliefs actually influence voters.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: We urgently need a major tax cut for our upper-income citizens.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
The present level of unemployment is the highest ever due to the recession.

A major tax cut for upper-income citizens would lead to a large increase in investment, thereby creating new jobs.

Without this measure, investment will not grow.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The citizen predicts a chain: a major tax cut for upper-income citizens, then a correspondingly large increase in investment, then new jobs. The conclusion that we urgently need the cut depends on that first step actually happening.

How could we argue the plan fails? Suppose upper-income citizens get the money and have no way to put it toward investment. Then the cut produces no investment, no new jobs, and no reason to call it urgent.

So the citizen needs, at a minimum, that the tax-cut money can go toward investment. It's a small requirement, but the whole plan rests on it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Expect a defender: an answer that rules out the objection "the tax-cut money can't end up as investment." It may be worded weakly, with "could" or "can." On Necessary Assumption, weak wording is a good sign, because the argument only needs the possibility to exist. Negate each choice and see whether the investment step breaks.

notes.body: The citizen says unemployment is the highest ever, not that the recession is the worst ever. Negate A: this recession is not the worst in the country's history. The tax-cut plan still works exactly as described, and record unemployment is still a reason to act quickly.

B is a sliding scale: the bigger the cut, the more likely people invest. The citizen needs only that this particular cut leads to investment. Negate B: a bigger cut does not make investing more likely. This major cut could still produce a large increase in investment, so the argument survives.
The argument is about whether this tax cut would make upper-income citizens invest. How their past investment compares with lower-income citizens' does not matter. Negate it and nothing changes.

Negate it: upper-income citizens could not use the tax-cut money in any way that increases investment. Then the "correspondingly large increase in investment" can't happen, the new jobs never come, and the case for the tax cut collapses.

Notice how little D claims. It doesn't say they will invest, only that they could. That's typical of a correct Necessary Assumption answer: the argument doesn't need a guarantee, but it can't survive if the outcome it predicts is impossible.
The citizen predicts what this tax cut will do. It does not need past tax cuts to have worked. Negate it, "past tax cuts did not tend to create jobs," and this one still could.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: We urgently need a major tax cut for our upper-income citizens.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body:
The present level of unemployment is the highest ever due to the recession.

A major tax cut for upper-income citizens would lead to a large increase in investment, thereby creating new jobs.

Without this measure, investment will not grow.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
The citizen is arguing for a specific solution to counter the effects of the recession, namely by proposing a tax cut. The premise that connects this solution to the desired effect (job creation) is that if upper-income citizens receive tax cuts, they will invest the extra money, thus creating new jobs.

For this argument to hold, the citizen is assuming that tax cuts for upper-income citizens will directly lead to increased investment. Put another way, the citizen assumes that the money saved from taxes will be used in a way that stimulates economic activity.

A potential objection could be that upper-income citizens might choose to save the extra money or spend it on non-investment ventures, which wouldn't create jobs. Therefore, for the citizen's argument to stand, there must be an assumed link between the tax cuts and increased investment.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: We need to identify an assumption that explicitly links tax cuts for upper-income earners to increased investment. An answer choice that confirms the reasoning that tax cuts will result in the behavior needed to support job growth (i.e., investing) is crucial.

old_notes.body: Option (A) is irrelevant to the logic of how a tax cut would lead to job creation. The severity of the recession doesn’t necessarily affect how the tax cut would be used for investment.
Option (B) suggests a generalized likelihood that bigger tax cuts lead to more investment but doesn’t specify the necessity of investment increasing solely due to the tax cut as argued.
The argument is about whether this tax cut would make upper-income citizens invest. How their past investment compares with lower-income citizens' does not matter. Negate it and nothing changes.

The correct answer should indicate that the money gained from a tax cut by upper-income citizens will indeed increase investment, which aligns with choice (D).

Choice (D) states that upper-income citizens could use the money gained from the tax cut in ways that increase investment. This directly connects the proposed tax cut to the likely behavior that would fulfill the citizen's ultimate goal: job creation through increased investment.
The citizen predicts what this tax cut will do. It does not need past tax cuts to have worked. Negate it, "past tax cuts did not tend to create jobs," and this one still could.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Genetic engineering is not unethical. rephrase: It's okay to do genetic engineering.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Selective breeding, as we've done with farm animals for millennia, is a crude form of genetic engineering.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The scientist argues by analogy. Selective breeding is a crude form of genetic engineering, and people have done it for millennia, so genetic engineering is not unethical.

What has to be true about selective breeding for that to work? It has to be acceptable. If selective breeding were itself unethical, showing that genetic engineering resembles it would only put genetic engineering in bad company. The millennia of practice don't settle that question either. A practice can be very old and still wrong.

There's a second gap: is choosing which animals breed really the same kind of thing as directly manipulating genetic codes? The scientist treats them as one category, and a critic could dispute that. But the first gap is the one the argument can't do without. The scientist never says selective breeding is ethical.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The answer will most likely protect the base of the analogy: selective breeding itself is not unethical. It could also defend the comparison, saying breeding and genetic-code manipulation are relevantly alike. Negate each choice and ask whether the scientist's evidence still clears genetic engineering.

notes.body: "Never" is far more than the argument needs. The scientist's evidence is about one kind of manipulation, selective breeding. Negate A: some manipulation of genetic codes is unethical, say, manipulation done to cause harm. The scientist can accept that and still argue that genetic engineering, like selective breeding, is not unethical.

B is tempting because it sounds like a defense of genetic engineering. But the scientist's evidence is selective breeding, something people did, not something nature accomplished. Negate B: some things nature accomplishes would be unethical to accomplish with science. The comparison between breeding and genetic engineering is untouched.

Negate it: "selective breeding for desired traits is unethical." Then the analogy turns against the scientist. Showing that genetic engineering is like selective breeding only puts it next to something unethical, and the millennia of practice just mean we've been doing something wrong for a long time. The conclusion falls.

The move: in an argument by analogy, the conclusion borrows a property from the comparison case. The argument has to assume the comparison case actually has that property.

The argument is about ethics, not usefulness. Negate D: selective breeding is not important for human survival. Breeding could still be ethical, and the analogy still works. Something can be unimportant and perfectly acceptable.

E makes two sweeping claims: science can do only what is natural, and nothing natural is unethical. The scientist relies on neither. Negate E, say, science can do some things that aren't natural, and the comparison between selective breeding and genetic engineering still stands.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: Genetic engineering is not unethical. rephrase: It's okay to do genetic engineering.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Selective breeding, as we've done with farm animals for millennia, is a crude form of genetic engineering.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
The author is arguing both by appeal to analogy and to tradition.
She's saying, "Since we've done genetic engineering for millennia, it's ok to keep doing it". This assumes that anything we've done for millennia couldn't be unethical.
That doesn't seem like sound logic. Slavery existed for centuries, if not millennia, and it is clearly unethical.
The other structure at play here is the argument by analogy, where we say, "Since these two things have X in common, they have Y in common." Let's look at the two things and what similarities they're meant to have in common:
Picking which farm animals Manipulating the genetic you want to use for breeding codes of organisms intended similarity 1: they're both a form of genetic engineering intended similarity 2: they're both ok (not unethical) We might dispute either of the intended similarities. Is it really fair to say that both of these things are genetic engineering? Or is this equivocation? One of them literally means manipulating the genetic code of a living organism. The other one is talking about organizing which two things will have sex. Is it really fair to say they're both ok? Who ever said that crude farm-based genetic engineering we've been doing for millennia is actually ethical?

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: The answer might deal with the "if we've been doing it a while, then it's ethical" missing link. It might deal with the author's assumption that farm-breeding and genetic-code-manipulation are really relevantly similar forms of genetic engineering. It might deal with a missing piece of the author's analogy: that farm-based selective breeding itself is ok / ethical.

old_notes.body: "Never unethical" covers every possible case. The scientist only needs selective breeding, and genetic engineering like it, to be acceptable.

This is the most popular wrong answer, and it is easy to see why: it sounds like a defense of genetic engineering. But the scientist's argument is about a long human *practice* (selective breeding), not about what nature does. Negate B and the argument still stands.

Negate it: "selective breeding for desired traits *is* unethical." Then pointing out that we have done it for millennia only shows we have been doing something wrong for a long time. It no longer clears genetic engineering, and the conclusion falls.
Whether selective breeding is important for survival says nothing about whether it is ethical.
A sweeping claim about science and nature that the argument never uses.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Soaking dried beans overnight before cooking them reduces cooking time.
However, cooking without presoaking yields plumper beans.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Therefore, when a bean dish's quality is more important than the need to cook that dish quickly, beans should not be presoaked.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The evidence gives a trade-off. Presoaking saves time. Skipping it gives plumper beans. The conclusion says that when quality matters more than speed, skip the soak.

Notice the jump. The evidence talks about plumper beans. The conclusion talks about the dish's quality. Those aren't the same idea. How could we argue against the author? Suppose plumper beans don't make a dish any better. Then the only real difference between the two methods is cooking time, and there's no quality reason to skip the soak.

So the author has to assume that plumper beans make for a better dish.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that links plumper beans to a better dish. When the conclusion brings in an idea the evidence never mentioned (quality), the gap is usually the link between the evidence's idea and that new one. Confirm it with the negation test: if plumper beans do nothing for a dish, the argument falls apart.

notes.body:
This is the link from the Evaluate step. Negate it: plumper beans do not enhance the quality of a dish. Then skipping the soak buys nothing on the quality side, and the conclusion has no support.

The pattern to repeat: find the idea that appears only in the conclusion (quality), find the idea it replaced in the evidence (plumper beans), and look for the answer that connects them.
B is too strong. The argument can allow that some dishes do better with faster cooking. It only says that when a bean dish's quality matters more than speed, the beans shouldn't be presoaked.
The argument never compares appearance with taste. Plumper beans could improve a dish for any reason, so the argument doesn't need appearance to be as important as taste.
The argument is only about whether to presoak the beans. It needs no claim about whether anything else in the dish gets presoaked.

E links plumpness to taste, but the conclusion is about a dish's quality. The argument doesn't need plumpness to work through taste: plumper beans could improve a dish's quality even if they taste no better.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Ample food and little exercise can skew the results of animal research.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Lab animals get ample food and little exercise. Many studies assume their subjects are healthy. The caloric restriction studies, for example, assume their animals were not overfed to begin with.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body: The skewing only happens if lab conditions make the animals *unhealthy*. If eating freely and exercising little left them perfectly healthy, the studies' assumption would be true, and nothing would be skewed. The scientist never says the conditions are bad for the animals.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: A link: ample food and little exercise can be unhealthy for lab animals.

notes.body: A reverses the relationship the scientist needs. The argument needs ample food and little exercise to be capable of making animals unhealthy. A instead says a restricted diet and plenty of exercise guarantee health. Negate A: animals on that regimen could still be unhealthy for some other reason. The lab conditions could still harm them and skew results, so the argument is untouched.

Negate it: "these conditions *cannot* be unhealthy for the animals." Then the animals are healthy, the studies' assumption holds, and there is nothing to skew the results.

The move: when the evidence describes a condition and the conclusion says it skews results, the argument has to assume the condition actually affects what the studies take for granted. Here, that's the animals' health.

The scientist's claim is about lab animals and the studies that use them. Negate C: it is unusual for animals outside labs to have ample food and little exercise. That doesn't change whether lab conditions can make lab animals unhealthy, so the argument stands.

D says some studies already account for differences in living conditions. The scientist only claims these factors can skew results. Negate D: no animal studies take those differences into account. The argument still works, so it doesn't depend on D.

E is about how consistent the animals' eating is from day to day. The argument turns on whether ample food and little exercise can harm their health. Negate E: animals with unlimited food vary a lot from day to day. That tells us nothing about whether they're healthy, so the argument is unaffected.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: Ample food and little exercise can skew the results of animal research.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Lab animals get ample food and little exercise. Many studies assume their subjects are healthy. The caloric restriction studies, for example, assume their animals were not overfed to begin with.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: The skewing only happens if lab conditions make the animals *unhealthy*. If eating freely and exercising little left them perfectly healthy, the studies' assumption would be true, and nothing would be skewed. The scientist never says the conditions are bad for the animals.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: A link: ample food and little exercise can be unhealthy for lab animals.

old_notes.body: This is the most popular wrong answer. It flips the scientist's idea: the scientist needs bad conditions to *cause* poor health, not good conditions to *guarantee* good health. A restricted diet and plenty of exercise could still leave an animal unhealthy for other reasons, and the argument would be fine.
Negate it: "these conditions *cannot* be unhealthy for the animals." Then the animals are healthy, the studies' assumption holds, and there is nothing to skew the results.
Animals outside the lab are not part of the argument.
What some studies take into account does not affect whether the conditions can skew results.
How steady their eating habits are says nothing about whether the habits are healthy.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Highly profitable corporations can save money by reducing the monitoring done by managers, as long as the employees are given strong incentives to keep working hard.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Highly profitable corporations can save money by giving their employees expensive bonuses.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body: To reach this conclusion about the employees at these particular corporations, we need to assume that there is a relationship between giving them strong incentives to keep working hard and giving them expensive bonuses. We have to assume that these bonuses would motivate them to keep working hard even when the managers aren't watching them closely.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Predict the bridge between "strong incentives" in the evidence and "expensive bonuses" in the conclusion: expensive bonuses work as strong incentives for these employees. Negate that, and the evidence's condition is never met by the bonuses, so nothing connects the bonuses to any savings and the conclusion loses its support.

Watch for two traps: an answer that makes bonuses the only way to save, and an answer that explains why the plan would work if it already worked.

notes.body: The argument is about what highly profitable corporations can do, not about how many corporations do it now. Negate A: many corporations give bonuses strong enough to keep employees working hard without monitoring. That doesn't hurt the argument at all, so the argument doesn't depend on A.

B explains why savings would happen: if bonuses save money, it's because they cut monitoring time. The argument only needs bonuses to be able to save money, not a claim about the reason behind every case of savings. Negate B: a corporation could save money with bonuses for some other reason. The conclusion still holds, since it only says the corporations can save money.

C is about whether these corporations actually have managers monitor much. The argument is about what they could save by reducing monitoring. Negate C: more valuable manager time doesn't make monitoring less likely. That fits the argument fine. Monitoring is still costly, and cutting it while keeping employees motivated still saves money.

This connects the two terms the argument swaps. The evidence says these corporations can save money by reducing monitoring, as long as employees get strong incentives. The conclusion says they can save money by giving expensive bonuses. D says expensive bonuses are strong incentives for exactly these employees. Negate it: the bonuses aren't strong incentives. Then the evidence's condition isn't met, and nothing in the argument shows the bonuses save any money.

The move: when the conclusion names a specific tool (expensive bonuses) and the evidence names a general requirement (strong incentives), the argument assumes the tool meets the requirement.

E is too strong. "Only if" makes expensive bonuses a requirement for any savings from reduced monitoring. The argument needs bonuses to be one way to supply strong incentives, not the only way. Negate E: a corporation could cut monitoring and save money using other incentives, like promotions. Bonuses could still work too, so the argument stands.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Highly profitable corporations can save money by reducing the monitoring done by managers, as long as the employees are given strong incentives to keep working hard.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: Highly profitable corporations can save money by giving their employees expensive bonuses.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: To reach this conclusion about the employees at these particular corporations, we need to assume that there is a relationship between giving them strong incentives to keep working hard and giving them expensive bonuses. We have to assume that these bonuses would motivate them to keep working hard even when the managers aren't watching them closely.

old_notes.body: This answer says only a few corporations currently give bonuses that provide strong enough incentives. The argument is about what highly profitable corporations could do to save money, not about what corporations currently do. Whether many or few corporations already use effective bonuses does not affect whether the strategy would work if implemented. The argument makes a prescriptive claim about a potential policy, and the current adoption rate of that policy is irrelevant to its potential effectiveness. Additionally, this answer does not specify whether the bonuses are expensive or whether the corporations are highly profitable.

This answer says if a corporation can save money by giving bonuses, it is because bonuses reduce monitoring time. Diagrammed: saves money via bonuses -> reduces monitoring. This uses the conclusion as the trigger (sufficient condition) and provides an explanation for why it works. But the argument needs to establish that the conclusion is true, not explain why it would be true if it were. A necessary assumption should be something that, if false, would destroy the argument. This answer, if negated ("it is not necessarily because of reduced monitoring"), does not destroy the argument — the argument has already established the monitoring-reduction mechanism in its premises.

This answer says the more valuable managers' time is, the less likely the corporation will have managers monitor employees. At highly profitable corporations (where managers' time is most valuable), this suggests monitoring is already minimal. If monitoring is already low, there is little monitoring to reduce, which means less potential savings from the bonus strategy. This weakens rather than supports the argument. The argument depends on highly profitable corporations currently spending substantial manager time on monitoring, so there is something to save by reducing it. An answer suggesting they already do not monitor much undermines the premise that monitoring savings are available.

This answer states that for employees of highly profitable corporations where monitoring is reduced, expensive bonuses constitute strong incentives to keep working hard. This is the precise bridge the argument needs. The evidence says corporations can save money by reducing monitoring if employees get strong incentives. The conclusion says they can save money by giving expensive bonuses. This assumption connects the two by establishing that expensive bonuses are strong incentives for the relevant employees. Negation test: if expensive bonuses do not constitute strong incentives for these employees, then giving bonuses would not replace the need for monitoring, and no money would be saved. The argument collapses.

This answer says corporations can save money by reducing monitoring only if employees receive expensive bonuses. The word "only" makes expensive bonuses the sole method for saving money through reduced monitoring. The argument only needs bonuses to be one effective method, not the only method. Maybe strong incentives could also come from stock options, promotions, or other rewards. The argument does not need to assume bonuses are the exclusive solution — it only needs to assume they are an effective one. Negation test: "Corporations can also save money through reduced monitoring using incentives other than expensive bonuses." This does not destroy the argument because bonuses can still work even if alternatives also work.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The purpose of government is to prevent individuals from injuring others in the pursuit of their own welfare.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: If most individuals take a reasoned approach to getting what they want, the power of government should be less.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body: As is sometimes the case in a Necessary Assumption question, this argument contains more than one gap in logic. There are several new concepts in the conclusion that are different from concepts discussed in the evidence. The evidence mentions "injuring others" in the pursuit of our own welfare. The conclusion shifts to "a reasoned approach" to getting what we want. Many people would agree that taking a reasoned approach to something involves not injuring others, but that might not always be true. If someone tries to physically attack me, it might be reasonable for me to injure that person to prevent them from hurting me. This argument assumes that for most people, taking a reasoned approach to getting what we want involves not injuring others in pursuit of our own welfare. The evidence also mentions "the purpose of government," while the conclusion discusses "the power of government." These are different things. The argument assumes that the power of government should be reduced if individuals do not need the government to fulfill its purpose. We can get a sense for the structure of the argument, including the assumptions it makes, by putting it all together like this: Most individuals who take a reasoned approach to getting what they want will not injure others in the pursuit of their own welfare, so they will not need the government to fulfill its purpose. And if most individuals do not need the government to fulfill its purpose, the power of government should be less.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Expect a link between the conclusion's new idea, a reasoned approach, and the evidence's idea, injuring others. Something like: people who take a reasoned approach are less likely to injure others. Negate it, and reasoned people need government's protection just as much, so there's no reason for government's power to shrink.

notes.body: The argument doesn't care how people come to take a reasoned approach. Its conclusion only says what should follow once most of them do. Negate A: governments alone can convince people to be reasonable. The conditional conclusion is untouched, so the argument doesn't need A.

B is about a cost of government doing its job: does it get in the way of people pursuing their own welfare? The argument never weighs that cost. Negate B: government can't serve its purpose without diminishing people's ability to promote their welfare. The link between reasoned people and less need for government is unaffected.

This is the link the Goal predicted. Government exists to prevent people from injuring others. The conclusion says government should have less power when most people take a reasoned approach. That only follows if reasoned people injure others less. Negate C: people who take a reasoned approach are just as likely to injure others as anyone else. Then a reasoned population needs government's protection just as much, and the case for less power falls apart.

The move: find the idea that appears only in the conclusion (a reasoned approach) and the idea it needs to connect to in the evidence (injuring others). The answer that ties them together is usually the required assumption.

D is about what happens to people who injure others afterward: do they get the same treatment back? The argument is about whether reasoned people need government to stop them from injuring others in the first place. Negate D: people who injure others are not eventually treated the same way. Nothing in the argument changes.

E is about the risk of being injured, not of injuring others. It also ties that risk to how much interest people have in their own welfare, not to whether they take a reasoned approach. Negate E and the argument is untouched: the theorist's case still turns on reasoned people injuring others less.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: If most individuals take a reasoned approach to getting what they want, the power of government should be less.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: As is sometimes the case in a Necessary Assumption question, this argument contains more than one gap in logic. There are several new concepts in the conclusion that are different from concepts discussed in the evidence. The evidence mentions "injuring others" in the pursuit of our own welfare. The conclusion shifts to "a reasoned approach" to getting what we want. Many people would agree that taking a reasoned approach to something involves not injuring others, but that might not always be true. If someone tries to physically attack me, it might be reasonable for me to injure that person to prevent them from hurting me. This argument assumes that for most people, taking a reasoned approach to getting what we want involves not injuring others in pursuit of our own welfare. The evidence also mentions "the purpose of government," while the conclusion discusses "the power of government." These are different things. The argument assumes that the power of government should be reduced if individuals do not need the government to fulfill its purpose. We can get a sense for the structure of the argument, including the assumptions it makes, by putting it all together like this: Most individuals who take a reasoned approach to getting what they want will not injure others in the pursuit of their own welfare, so they will not need the government to fulfill its purpose. And if most individuals do not need the government to fulfill its purpose, the power of government should be less.

old_notes.body: Whether governments can convince individuals to be reasonable is not part of the argument. The evidence is about government preventing injury; the conclusion is about what happens if people are reasonable. How people become reasonable is outside the scope.

Whether government can serve its purpose without diminishing people's ability to promote their welfare is not required by the argument. The argument is about what happens when people are reasonable — not about how government exercises its power. Even if government sometimes diminishes people's welfare while preventing injury, the argument's logic would still hold.

This bridges the central gap. The evidence says government exists to prevent people from injuring others. The conclusion says reasonable people need less government. The missing link: reasonable people are less likely to injure others. If this is not true — if reasonable people injure others just as often — then being reasonable would not reduce the need for government's injury-prevention purpose. Negating this assumption destroys the argument.

Whether people who injure others will be treated the same way is about reciprocity or karma, not about the argument's logic. The argument concerns the relationship between reasonable behavior and government power, not what happens to people who injure others.

The argument discusses people injuring others. Whether interest in one's own welfare affects the likelihood of being injured oneself is a different question. The evidence is about preventing people from committing injury, not about factors that make people more or less likely to be victims.
